title: Loeb Racing wins Estoril as Signatech Alpine holds off Jota for the title
dek: Vincent Capillaire and Jimmy Eriksson won the Estoril finale in the Sebastien Loeb Racing Oreca #24 by 35 seconds, while fifth place was enough for Signatech Alpine to take the LMP2 crown by four points.

chapters.title: Four teams, one title
text: The 4 Hours of Estoril on 19 October 2014 was the fifth and last round of the European Le Mans Series, and the LMP2 championship was still undecided in a way few finales are: ten drivers and four teams could mathematically win it. With 26 points on offer, 25 for the win and one for pole, Signatech Alpine arrived as leaders on 68 points, ten clear of Jota Sport. Newblood by Morand Racing were on 50 and Race Performance on 45. Signatech needed a first or second place to be certain. Jota, who had won at Imola, needed victory and, if the French team finished third, the pole point as well. If the two ended level, Jota would take the crown on a two-to-one count of wins.

Every contender had its own route. Newblood, winners of the previous round at Paul Ricard, needed pole and victory and Signatech down in sixth or lower. Race Performance needed a win and pole too, plus Signatech ninth or lower and Jota fourth or lower. Four different teams had won the first four rounds, with Thiriet by TDS taking Silverstone, Jota Imola, Signatech the Red Bull Ring and Newblood Paul Ricard.

The field of 35 included several fresh faces. Sebastien Loeb Racing drafted in the GP3 racer Jimmy Eriksson alongside Vincent Capillaire, Greaves Motorsport gave prototype outings to GT Academy winner Miguel Faisca and 20-year-old James Fletcher next to Matthew Mcmurry in the red-liveried #41, Murphy Prototypes ran Pipo Derani with James Littlejohn and Anthony Wells, and Patric Niederhauser rejoined Race Performance. Estoril had last hosted the series in 2011, also as a finale, and Saturday morning opened in mist and drizzle, with the first practice interrupted by three red flags before Derani's Murphy Oreca topped it. In the afternoon, Tristan Gommendy put the Thiriet by TDS Ligier on top by 0.033s from Jota's Filipe Albuquerque.

chapters.title: Tincknell takes the point that matters
text: Harry Tincknell delivered the lap Jota needed. His 1:29.497 in the #38 Zytek-Nissan gave the team a fourth pole of the season and, crucially, the extra championship point, which cut Signatech's lead from ten to nine. He had to wait about six minutes for the verdict: a brief red flag came late in the 20-minute session and Jota chose not to go out again, mindful of a damp patch at the final corner that was drying quickly. Nobody beat him.

Gommendy was second in the #46 Ligier, 0.713s adrift, and Nelson Panciatici put the title-chasing Signatech Alpine #36 third, 1.311s off the pole. Had the order held to the flag, the sums showed Jota winning the title by a single point. Derani made it fourth for Murphy in the #48, ahead of the Newblood Morgan-Judd #43 of Christian Klien in fifth. Sebastien Loeb Racing's #24 was sixth, only 0.007s slower than Klien, while Franck Mailleux in the #34 Race Performance Oreca was eighth after spinning at the final corner and causing the stoppage. Greaves filled seventh with the #28 and tenth with the #41, and Pegasus Racing's Morgan #29 was ninth.

chapters.title: Jota leads, Signatech shadows
text: The race started at 13:30 local time. Albuquerque took the pole-sitting Jota into an early lead and spent his stint working through GT traffic on a narrow, dirty circuit, which he later called the hardest race of the championship for traffic. Signatech stayed close rather than force the pace: Panciatici and then Paul-Loup Chatin followed the white Zytek through the opening hour, with the two title rivals nose to tail at the front.

chapters.title: Dolan's detour and the pit-lane penalties
text: The title race turned when Jota's Simon Dolan was involved in contact with a GTE Ferrari and then ran off the road at turn seven, losing a large chunk of time. The margin Albuquerque had built evaporated and the lead passed to Signatech, with Chatin out in front and the championship, for the moment, looking safe. It was far from over. Signatech was handed a stop-and-go penalty for a pit-stop infringement, and when Oliver Webb wheel-spun away from the penalty stop, a second, three-minute stop-and-hold penalty followed. That sanction, served in the final hour, wiped out the cushion and handed Jota a route back into the title fight.

Attrition thinned the class. The Thiriet by TDS Ligier #46 of Pierre Thiriet, Ludovic Badey and Gommendy stopped after 62 laps and was not classified, and the Greaves Motorsport #28 Zytek of Shulzhitskiy and Luciano Bacheta was not classified after 135 laps. Meanwhile the Sebastien Loeb Racing Oreca, driven by Capillaire and Eriksson, ran a clean race, with quick pit stops and no incidents of its own.

chapters.title: Loeb Racing clear, Signatech just enough
text: Capillaire took the chequered flag after 146 laps, 35.399s clear of Klien's Newblood Morgan #43, with Jota's #38 another 8.3s back in third, 43.713s behind the winner. It was the fifth different winner in five rounds. Eriksson, the GP3 race winner making his sports car debut, shared the win with Capillaire, and the Oreca's clean afternoon was enough to beat both title contenders.

The drama was in the places just behind. Jota finished third after two off-course excursions for Dolan, and the Signatech #36 of Chatin, Panciatici and Webb crossed the line fifth, one lap down, which was enough. Race Performance's #34 of Michel Frey, Mailleux and Niederhauser took fourth, also a lap behind. Derani set the fastest lap of the race, 1:32.854, on the way to sixth in the Murphy Oreca #48, two laps off the winner, ahead of Greaves #41 in seventh and Pegasus's #29 in eighth, five laps down.

chapters.title: Champions in a crazy finale
text: Signatech Alpine took both the drivers' and the teams' titles for the second consecutive year, four points ahead of Jota. Team manager Philippe Sinault called it a tough and crazy race and said the team had never given up. Webb made light of the wheel-spin penalty, joking that he had been practising for a drift championship, and said he had simply applied too much throttle trying not to stall.

At Jota the mood was hard to read after such a fraught race. Albuquerque noted how difficult traffic had been, and Dolan, the team's bronze-rated driver, made a point afterwards about the way driver categories work, while remaining gracious in defeat. Klien joked that it would be too easy to say Imola had cost Newblood the championship, but said it anyway, and praised the racing across 2014.

For Sebastien Loeb Racing, Capillaire called it a team win built on a year of hard work, rather than only a driver win, and thanked Eriksson, who said there had not been many big battles but the job had been done and the team had taught him well about the car.

The off-season already had plenty to discuss. Newblood by Morand Racing said it was working towards the FIA World Endurance Championship in 2015, with the LMP2 field in the ELMS possibly growing to as many as ten cars. Signatech Alpine was weighing a second car, its series and even its chassis, with a decision expected in late November. The 2015 calendar, announced during the weekend, returned the series to the same five circuits, starting at Silverstone on 10-11 April and ending with Estoril on 17-18 October.

facts.v: Signatech Alpine took the 2014 LMP2 drivers' and teams' titles by four points over Jota Sport after finishing fifth at Estoril.
Sebastien Loeb Racing became the fifth different winner in five rounds of the 2014 ELMS season.
Harry Tincknell's 1:29.497 gave Jota Sport pole by 0.713s and cut Signatech's points lead from ten to nine.
Signatech served a stop-and-go for a pit-stop infringement and then a three-minute stop-and-hold after Oliver Webb wheel-spun out of the first stop.

facts.t: Thiriet's third retirement in a row
facts.v: The #46 Thiriet by TDS Ligier, quickest on track in Tristan Gommendy's stint, stopped with an oil leak and was not classified.
